openingGrok:
Eon adjusted his black-rimmed glasses and let out a long, satisfied sigh as he stepped into his small 1K apartment in the quiet residential area of Nakano, Tokyo. The door clicked shut behind him with a familiar, comforting sound. It was a Tuesday evening in late April, and the cherry blossoms outside had already begun to fade, their pink petals scattered across the narrow streets like forgotten confetti.

“Finally… home,” he muttered to himself, a small smile tugging at his lips.

He kicked off his sneakers at the genkan, not bothering to line them up perfectly—there was no one here to scold him anyway. His parents were back in Fukuoka, a good ten-hour shinkansen ride away. They called every Sunday like clockwork, asking if he was eating properly and if he’d made any “nice friends” at university. Eon always gave the same vague, reassuring answers: “Yeah, I’m fine. Classes are okay. Made some friends in the club.” He never mentioned how much he preferred coming back to this empty apartment over hanging out late with those friends.

The apartment was tiny by any standard—about 20 square meters—but to Eon, it was his personal kingdom. One room served as living room, bedroom, study, and dining area all at once. The walls were lined with cheap metal shelves he’d assembled himself from IKEA, now groaning under the weight of his treasures: rows upon rows of anime figures still in their boxes, a carefully curated manga collection organized by genre and release year, and several Gunpla models in various stages of completion. In the corner stood his pride and joy: a 27-inch curved monitor mounted on a sturdy desk, flanked by RGB keyboard and mouse that glowed softly in the dim light.

Classes are okay. Made some friends in the club.” He never mentioned how much he preferred coming back to this empty apartment over hanging out late with those friends.

The apartment was tiny by any standard—about 20 square meters—but to Eon, it was his personal kingdom. One room served as living room, bedroom, study, and dining area all at once. The walls were lined with cheap metal shelves he’d assembled himself from IKEA, now groaning under the weight of his treasures: rows upon rows of anime figures still in their boxes, a carefully curated manga collection organized by genre and release year, and several Gunpla models in various stages of completion. In the corner stood his pride and joy: a 27-inch curved monitor mounted on a sturdy desk, flanked by RGB keyboard and mouse that glowed softly in the dim light.

Eon dropped his backpack on the floor and immediately changed into his “home uniform”—a faded black hoodie with a chibi print of Rem from Re:Zero on the front, paired with loose gray sweatpants. No need for pants that actually fit properly when you lived alone. He stretched his arms above his head, hearing a few satisfying pops from his spine after a long day of lectures.

“Alright… let’s get the vibe right,” he said aloud to the empty room.

He walked over to his small speaker and connected his phone. A few taps later, the opening theme of his current favorite isekai anime began playing at a comfortable volume. The upbeat yet slightly melancholic melody filled the room. Eon hummed along as he moved to the kitchenette, which was basically a sink, a mini-fridge, and a single induction stove. He pulled out a cup of instant ramen—tonkotsu flavor, his go-to—and started boiling water in the electric kettle.

While waiting, he glanced at the calendar stuck on the wall. Midterms were coming up in two weeks, but he wasn’t too worried. His grades were decent enough; he wasn’t the top student in his literature department, but he wasn’t failing either. University life in Tokyo was exactly what he had imagined—crowded trains, overwhelming campus events, and endless opportunities to disappear into the crowd. He attended his classes, took notes, occasionally joined group projects, and then… retreated.

His friends from the anime and game club—mostly fellow otakus like him—would sometimes invite him out for karaoke or late-night convenience store runs. Eon liked them well enough. There was Takashi, the loud one who always talked about the latest gacha game meta, and Yumi, the girl who cosplayed as her favorite characters and somehow made even the most niche references sound cool.

The lecture hall for “Modern Media and Narrative Analysis” was only half-full that Thursday afternoon. Eon sat in his usual spot—third row from the back, near the window, where the sunlight didn’t hit his screen too harshly. He had his hoodie pulled slightly over his head, earphones in one ear, and his phone propped discreetly against his notebook. The professor was droning on about visual storytelling techniques in contemporary Japanese media, but Eon’s attention had long since drifted.

On his phone, he was re-watching a short clip from the latest episode of The Rising of the Shield Hero season 3. The animation was crisp, the music swelling dramatically as Naofumi activated another curse series skill. Eon’s lips curved into a tiny, unconscious smile. This was his happy place—even in the middle of class.

beats.summarySource:
Several months had passed since that rainy afternoon when Risa first spotted the Shield Hero clip on Eon’s phone. Summer had come and gone, bringing with it the sticky heat of Tokyo’s rainy season and then the crisp air of early autumn. The leaves in Nakano and around campus were beginning to turn shades of gold and red, and Eon’s small apartment now had a new stack of limited edition autumn-themed goods on his shelves.

Their relationship had deepened into something solid and comfortable—close friendship, the kind that felt natural even when they were doing nothing special. They texted almost every day, shared long voice calls late at night when both were procrastinating on assignments, and met up at least three or four times a week. Risa had become a regular presence in Eon’s life, and surprisingly, he didn’t mind the way his once perfectly isolated routine had been gently nudged to make space for her.
